---
title: Supporting Python packages
---

Course notebooks often need code that is important for the activity but not
important for students to read in that moment. A small Python package inside
the course repository gives that code a stable home and lets notebooks use a
short, intentional interface.

This pattern is useful for:

- A complex method whose implementation would distract from the scientific
  question being studied.
- A function that students write in an earlier session and reuse later.
- Interactive widgets whose internal event handling is not the learning goal.
- Dataset loaders, plotting helpers, answer checks, and environment-specific
  compatibility code.
- Shared definitions that would otherwise be copied between notebooks.

The package remains part of the course and is maintained with it. It does not
need to be published to the Python Package Index (PyPI).

For related setup, see [Pixi configuration](pixi-configuration.qmd),
[Project scripts](scripts.qmd), [Python code cells](../code_interactive/python-code-cells.qmd),
and [Notebooks](../code_interactive/notebooks.qmd).

## Keep the learning objective visible

A package should remove incidental complexity, not hide the subject students
are meant to learn. Before moving code into a package, ask whether students
should be able to explain, modify, or implement it.

For example, students might derive and implement a fitting function in one
session. A later session can import the tested function while focusing on
experimental design. The earlier implementation remains available in the
course material or linked source, but it no longer has to be repeated in every
notebook.

Treat imported course functions as a small public API:

- Give functions names that make sense in the teaching context.
- Use predictable inputs and return values.
- Add concise docstrings and type annotations where they improve comprehension.
- Avoid hidden global state and surprising import-time behavior.
- Link to the source when interested students may benefit from reading it.

::: {.callout-tip title="Package stable scaffolding"}
Keep exploratory code and the code students are expected to write in the
notebook. Package stable scaffolding that is reused or would otherwise obscure
the activity.
:::

## Two course examples

The existing course packages illustrate different useful sizes:

- [`molecular_biology_II/course-utils`](https://github.com/au-mbg/molecular-biology-II/tree/main/course-utils)
  is deliberately small. It supplies answer-checking behavior and a Pyodide
  compatibility patch used by a ChIP-seq notebook.
- [`fysisk_biokemi/course-utils`](https://github.com/au-mbg/fysisk-biokemi/tree/main/course-utils)
  is a broader library of datasets, reusable analysis functions, and
  interactive widgets used across lessons and exercises.

Start small. A package can grow when genuinely shared needs appear; creating a
large abstraction before the course uses it makes maintenance harder.

## Create a minimal package

Place the package in a directory such as `course-utils/` beside the course
material:

```text
course-repository/
├── course/
│   └── lessons/
├── course-utils/
│   ├── pyproject.toml
│   ├── README.md
│   ├── src/
│   │   └── course_utils/
│   │       ├── __init__.py
│   │       └── calculations.py
│   └── tests/
│       └── test_calculations.py
└── pixi.toml
```

The `src` layout ensures notebooks import the installed package rather than
accidentally importing directly from the source directory. The
[Python Packaging User Guide](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/tutorials/packaging-projects/)
and [uv build-backend documentation](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/build-backend/)
describe this layout in more detail.

### Package metadata

Create `course-utils/pyproject.toml`:

```toml
[project]
name = "course-utils"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Supporting utilities for the example course"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = []

[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.12,<0.13"]
build-backend = "uv_build"
```

The distribution name is `course-utils`, as it will appear in installation
commands and wheel filenames. Python imports use the normalized module name
`course_utils`; hyphens are not valid in an import statement.

The `uv_build` backend is a good fit for a pure-Python course package and uses
`src/course_utils` by default. Packages containing compiled extensions require
a different build backend and platform-specific build process, which is
outside this introductory pattern.

### Define a public helper

Put the implementation in `src/course_utils/calculations.py`:

```python
def dilution_volume(
    initial_concentration: float,
    final_concentration: float,
    final_volume: float,
) -> float:
    """Return the stock volume required for a dilution."""
    if initial_concentration <= 0:
        raise ValueError("initial_concentration must be positive")
    if final_concentration < 0 or final_volume < 0:
        raise ValueError("final values cannot be negative")

    return final_concentration * final_volume / initial_concentration
```

Export the intended public interface from `src/course_utils/__init__.py`:

```python
from .calculations import dilution_volume

__all__ = ["dilution_volume"]
```

Notebooks can now use a stable, readable import without depending on the
internal file layout:

```python
from course_utils import dilution_volume

stock_volume = dilution_volume(100, 10, 25)
```

## Install it in the Pixi environment

Install the repository copy as an editable PyPI dependency in the root
`pixi.toml`:

```toml
[pypi-dependencies]
course-utils = { path = "course-utils", editable = true }
```

Editable installation means changes under `course-utils/src/` are available
without rebuilding a wheel. Pixi records the package as part of the course
environment, so local previews, renders, and notebooks all import the same
code.

Run a quick import check after changing the environment:

```bash
pixi run python -c "from course_utils import dilution_volume; print(dilution_volume(100, 10, 25))"
```

### Place dependencies deliberately

Libraries required whenever the installed package runs belong in
`[project].dependencies`. Tools used only to render or maintain the course,
such as Quarto or a formatter, belong in the surrounding Pixi environment.

Use optional dependencies when delivery environments need different sets:

```toml
[project.optional-dependencies]
standard = [
    "ipywidgets>=8.1",
    "matplotlib>=3.10",
]
pyodide = [
    "ipywidgets",
    "matplotlib",
]
```

The `fysisk_biokemi` package uses this approach to distinguish its standard
teaching environment from browser-based Python. Avoid duplicating a dependency
between Pixi and the package unless both layers genuinely use it independently.

## Add a small test

Moving code out of a notebook makes it reusable, but it also makes breakage
less visible. Test the public behavior in
`course-utils/tests/test_calculations.py`:

```python
import pytest

from course_utils import dilution_volume


def test_dilution_volume() -> None:
    assert dilution_volume(100, 10, 25) == 2.5


def test_initial_concentration_must_be_positive() -> None:
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        dilution_volume(0, 10, 25)
```

Add `pytest` to a development environment or the root Pixi dependencies and
expose the test through a task:

```toml
[tasks.test-course-utils]
cmd = "pytest course-utils/tests"
```

Run the package tests after changing shared behavior, then render at least one
representative document that imports it. Tests can verify a calculation, but
they do not show whether a widget renders correctly or whether its instructions
still make sense. See [Project scripts](scripts.qmd) for broader repository
checks.

## Distribute the package to students

Editable installation is ideal for maintainers, but student notebooks may run
outside the course repository. Choose a distribution method that matches that
environment.

### Install from the course repository

An ordinary Python environment with Git available can install the package
directly from its subdirectory:

```bash
python -m pip install "course-utils @ git+https://github.com/ORGANISATION/COURSE.git@main#subdirectory=course-utils"
```

Pin a tag or commit instead of `main` when a notebook must remain reproducible.
This method gives students the source distribution and asks their environment
to build it during installation.

### Build a wheel

A wheel is a ready-to-install package archive. It avoids requiring Git and
makes the exact distributed version visible in the filename. Add `uv` to a
development Pixi environment and provide build tasks:

```toml
[tasks.build-course-utils]
cmd = "rm -rf dist && uv build --wheel course-utils --out-dir dist"
description = "Build the course utility wheel"

[tasks.check-course-utils-wheel]
cmd = "uvx pkginfo dist/*.whl"
description = "Inspect the built wheel metadata"
```

`uv build` creates a filename such as
`course_utils-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl`. The `py3-none-any` tags indicate a
pure-Python wheel that is not tied to one operating system or CPU architecture.
See the official [uv build documentation](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/build/)
for the build process.

Publish the wheel under the course site's `wheels/` directory. For example,
copy the validated wheel into the Quarto project before its Pages artifact is
uploaded and include the directory as a project resource:

```yaml
# _quarto.yml
project:
  resources:
    - wheels/**
```

The deployed wheel then has a stable HTTPS URL such as:

```text
https://ORGANISATION.github.io/COURSE/wheels/course_utils-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
```

A raw GitHub URL to a committed wheel is also possible, as used by
`molecular_biology_II`, but publishing versioned wheels with the course site
keeps student downloads with the rest of the deployed material.

### Bootstrap a hosted notebook

A notebook can use the local editable package when it is already available and
fall back to the published wheel elsewhere:

```python
try:
    import course_utils
except ImportError:
    %pip install -q https://ORGANISATION.github.io/COURSE/wheels/course_utils-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
    import course_utils
```

Pin the wheel version in teaching material. Whenever distributed behavior
changes:

1. Update and test the package code.
2. Increment the version in `pyproject.toml`.
3. Build and inspect the new wheel.
4. Publish it with the course site.
5. Update notebook installation URLs.
6. Test in a clean student environment.

Changing code without changing the version and URL makes browser and notebook
caches difficult to reason about.

## Colab and browser-based Python

Google Colab is an ordinary hosted Python environment. It can generally
install a pure-Python wheel or install from Git, subject to network access and
the package's declared Python requirements. A wheel is usually faster and
more predictable for students.

Pyodide runs Python as WebAssembly in the browser. Its package installer can
load pure-Python wheels and packages for which compatible Pyodide builds exist;
an ordinary wheel containing compiled desktop extensions will not work. See
the [micropip documentation](https://micropip.pyodide.org/) and the handbook's
[Pyodide guidance](../code_interactive/quarto-live-pyodide.qmd).

For a browser notebook, publish the wheel over HTTPS and request the Pyodide
extras when needed:

```python
%pip install -q "course-utils[pyodide] @ https://ORGANISATION.github.io/COURSE/wheels/course_utils-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl"
```

Test this installation in the actual browser environment. A successful local
Pixi import does not prove that all dependencies are available in Pyodide.

Environment patches sometimes belong in a course package. For example,
`molecular_biology_II` adapts HTTP CSV loading when running under Pyodide. Keep
such behavior platform-gated, documented, and idempotent so importing the
package twice has the same effect as importing it once. Prefer an explicit
setup function over import-time side effects unless every consumer genuinely
requires the patch.

## Package data and widgets

Small datasets, templates, or static files can live inside the import package
and be read with `importlib.resources`. This makes them travel with the wheel
instead of relying on the notebook's working directory. The
`fysisk_biokemi.datasets` module uses this pattern for course datasets.

Widgets are also strong package candidates when their internal code would
overwhelm the lesson. Keep the notebook-facing call small, for example:

```python
from course_utils.widgets import dilution_helper

dilution_helper()
```

Test widgets in every intended frontend: local Jupyter, rendered Quarto
output, Colab, or Pyodide may support different widget libraries and transport
mechanisms.

## Maintenance checklist

Before relying on a course package for a new teaching period:

1. Run its tests in a clean Pixi environment.
2. Render representative student and solution documents that import it.
3. Build the wheel and inspect its metadata and contents.
4. Install the wheel into a clean Python environment and run an import check.
5. Test each hosted environment, especially Colab or Pyodide, separately.
6. Confirm that published notebook URLs refer to the current package version.
7. Check widgets, bundled datasets, and other non-code resources manually.

A supporting package reduces duplication, but it also creates shared code on
which many lessons may depend. Keep its interface small, version distributed
changes, and test the same artifact that students will install.
